summary.text: A microbe is an organism of microscopic size, living either as a single cell or as a colony of cells.
Microbes live everywhere from the poles to the equator, in deserts, geysers, rocks and the deep sea, and they make up the microbiota found in and on all multicellular organisms.
Their study began with Leeuwenhoek's microscope in the 1670s, and Pasteur and Koch later showed that microbes cause food spoilage and diseases such as tuberculosis and anthrax.

items.prompt: A scientist boils a broth so nothing living is left, then shields it from particles in the air. Nothing grows. What does this suggest about life that appears in unshielded broth?

options.label: It forms by itself out of the broth's own contents
It arrives from outside, carried as spores on dust
It survives the boiling and multiplies afterwards
It is created by the heat of the boiling itself

items.explain: Boiling left no microorganisms, and shielded broth stayed empty, so the growth in other broths came from outside, as spores on dust.

items.prompt: A vet finds the same bacterium in every sick cow. Blood from a sick cow injected into a healthy one makes that cow ill too. What has the vet shown?

options.label: That the microbe is a harmless bystander in sick cows
That the illness comes from the blood and not the microbe
That the healthy cow was already carrying the illness
Good evidence that the microbe causes the disease

items.explain: Koch's anthrax work followed this pattern: a microbe found in the sick, then illness after transfer to a healthy animal, supports a causal link.

items.prompt: An oak tree is huge and made of many cells. A student says it belongs to a domain that holds only microbes. Why is that wrong?

options.label: All multicellular organisms belong to the domain Eukaryota
Trees are too old to be grouped with any microbes
Only Archaea contain organisms of any large size
Large organisms sit outside the three domains of life

items.explain: Two domains, Archaea and Bacteria, contain only microorganisms, while Eukaryota includes all multicellular organisms.

items.prompt: Explorers find single-celled life in a scalding geyser pool and on the deep sea floor. What does this fit best?

options.label: Such places hold no life, so the cells must be visitors
Only one hardy microbe lives in every extreme place
Microbes inhabit very different places, some adapted to extremes
Microbes cannot live far from fertile soil and gardens

items.explain: Microorganisms live from the poles to the equator, in geysers and the deep sea, and some are adapted to very hot, cold or high-pressure conditions.

items.prompt: A single-celled organism makes food from light like a plant, yet swims about like an animal. What did finds like this lead to in the 1860s?

options.label: Its placement in the plant kingdom alone
The naming of a third kingdom
Its placement in the animal kingdom alone
Its dismissal as a mistake in observation

items.explain: Euglena was photosynthetic like plants but motile like animals, so it fit neither kingdom, which led to a third kingdom being named.

items.prompt: A friend says every microbe on your body is an enemy to wash away. What is wrong with that?

options.label: Washing cannot remove any microbe from the body
Microbes on the body only exist when you are ill
Hygiene measures target nothing that can cause disease
Some, like the gut flora, are an essential part of the body

items.explain: The human microbiota includes essential gut flora, while hygiene measures are aimed at the pathogens that cause infectious disease.

beats.title: Who Blamed the Dust?
beats.hook: Nobody could see them, yet careful experiments put microbes on trial and found them guilty.

beats.prompt: You boil a broth so nothing living is left, then let air reach it only through a curved tube where dust settles on the way. What grows in the broth?
beats.explain: Pasteur's boiled broths stayed empty, so living things in other broths came from outside as spores on dust.

choices.label: Living things appear on their own
choices.feedback: This is spontaneous generation, which tempts because broth looks like food for life, but boiling had left no microorganisms inside.

choices.label: Only a thin layer grows near the tube
choices.feedback: It seems the air should bring something in, but the tube let dust settle before it reached the broth.

beats.prompt: Put these ideas about unseen disease-causing life in order of when they appeared.

items.label: Avicenna suggests tuberculosis and other diseases might be contagious
Fracastoro proposes transferable seedlike entities cause epidemics
Hooke's Micrographia coins the term cell
Leeuwenhoek experiments with microorganisms using his own microscopes

beats.prompt: Match each scientist to what they showed or did.

right.label: Coined the term cell in Micrographia
Experimented with microorganisms using single-lensed microscopes
Refuted spontaneous generation with boiled broths
Showed bacteria in infected cattle blood cause anthrax

beats.explain: Each one moved the study of microorganisms forward with a different observation or experiment.

beats.prompt: This reasoning about Pasteur's experiment has one wrong step. Which?

steps.text: Pasteur boiled his broths first, so no microorganisms survived inside them.
Nothing grew in the broths during his experiment.
So the living things in other broths came from outside, as spores on dust.
So the experiment supported the theory of spontaneous generation.

beats.explain: Because nothing grew, the experiment refuted spontaneous generation and supported the germ theory of disease.

beats.idea: Experiments showed that living microorganisms, not spontaneous generation, cause spoilage and disease.

paragraphs.heading: What a microbe is
paragraphs.text: A microorganism, or microbe, is a living thing of microscopic size. It may live as a single cell or as a colony of cells. Microbes make up most single-celled life across all three domains of life. Two of those domains, Archaea and Bacteria, contain nothing but microbes, while the third, Eukaryota, holds many single-celled protists and protozoans as well as every many-celled organism. Some many-celled organisms are microscopic too, such as micro-animals and some fungi and algae.

paragraphs.heading: Where they live
paragraphs.text: Microbes live in deserts, geysers, rocks and the deep sea, and from the poles to the equator. Some are built for great heat or cold and others for high pressure, while a few, Deinococcus radiodurans among them, handle heavy radiation. They are a vital part of fertile soil, and they form the microbiota found in and on every multicellular organism. Rocks in Australia 3.45 billion years old show that they once held microbes, the earliest direct evidence of life on Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Guessing at unseen life
paragraphs.text: People wondered about invisible life for many centuries before anyone saw it. By the 6th century BC, Jains in what is now India described tiny beings called nigodas, said to be born in clusters, to live everywhere, and to last only a fraction of a second. In 1020, in The Canon of Medicine, Avicenna proposed that tuberculosis and other illnesses might be contagious. In 1546, Girolamo Fracastoro proposed that epidemics came from seedlike entities passed on by direct or indirect contact, or even across long distances without contact.

paragraphs.heading: First sight under the lens
paragraphs.text: The scientific study of microbes began in the 1670s, when Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw them under the microscope. In 1673 he became the first to find and experiment on them, using simple single-lens microscopes he designed himself, and he is counted among the fathers of microbiology. Robert Hooke, working at the same time, also used a microscope to see microbial life, in the form of mould fruiting bodies. In his 1665 book Micrographia he drew what he studied and coined the word cell.

paragraphs.heading: Pasteur and the boiled broth
paragraphs.text: In the 1850s Louis Pasteur showed that microbes make food spoil. He boiled broths so nothing living survived in them, then let air reach them in vessels that kept dust away, either with a filter or with a curved tube where the dust settled. Nothing grew. So the life that normally appears in such broths arrives from outside, as spores on dust, instead of arising inside by itself. That result overturned the theory of spontaneous generation and backed the germ theory of disease.

paragraphs.heading: Koch and anthrax
paragraphs.text: In 1876 Robert Koch showed that microbes can cause disease. The blood of cattle sick with anthrax always held large numbers of Bacillus anthracis, and a small sample of it injected into a healthy animal made that animal ill. Bacteria he grew in a nutrient broth did the same. From these tests he drew up criteria for linking a microbe to a disease, now called Koch's postulates; they do not fit every case, but they are still used. In the 1880s he also found the microbes behind tuberculosis, cholera, diphtheria and anthrax.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter to us
paragraphs.text: Microbes touch human life in many ways. They ferment foods, treat sewage, and produce fuel, enzymes and other compounds. Biologists rely on them as model organisms, and they have also been used in biological warfare and bioterrorism. Inside the body they form the human microbiota, including the essential gut flora, while the pathogens behind many infectious diseases are microbes too, which is why hygiene measures target them.
